paper_style.palette_strategy: Main method diagrams use teal Context/Cache Attention and yellow Query Attention; locality maps use a green sequential scale; LPD is repeatedly accented in red in plots and cyan in result rows. Natural image montages use incidental image colors with red edit boxes. The table accent is method-row highlighting rather than a universal metric palette.
paper_style.vector_raster_mix: The 24-page PDF mixes vector text/rules/most diagrams and charts with raster attention maps and image montages. Figure 1 and Figure 12 match public PNG assets; Figures 2, 10, 11, 12, and 13 contain raster image content, while Figures 3–8, 9, and 14 are primarily vector/text compositions. All 24 pages were rendered as 1530×1980 PNGs at 180 dpi for inspection.
paper_style.style_consistency: Nimbus Roman/Computer Modern dominate captions, body text, and tables; Helvetica Neue-like text appears inside diagrams and plots. Bold caption titles are consistent for main figures/tables and Figures 12–14, while title-only Figure 10/11 captions are weaker. Teal/yellow masks, green locality maps, red LPD marks, and cyan LPD table rows form a recognizable but locally scoped visual system.

figures.label: Figure 1

caption.text: Figure 1: Performance comparison among parallelized autoregressive models on ImageNet 256×256. We significantly reduce the generation steps and achieve at least 3.4x lower latency compared with previous models.

color.semantic_mapping: Gray bubbles identify prior NAR/PAR/RandAR/ARPG points; red and green bubbles identify LPD at 20 and 32 steps; bubble size indicates the 350M/700M/1.4B scale key.

plot_grammar.legend_placement: upper-left scale key plus direct method labels

encodings.y: Fréchet Inception Distance (FID), lower is better
encodings.color: Gray baselines versus red/green LPD points
encodings.shape: Circular bubble; area encodes model scale
encodings.line: Dotted red arrows annotate 4.2x and 3.4x faster
encodings.text: NAR, PAR, RandAR, ARPG, LPD (20/32 steps), and 350M/700M/1.4B

figures.data_and_statistics: Single-point ImageNet 256×256 quality–latency positioning for NAR, PAR, RandAR, ARPG, and LPD. The plotted LPD points include 20-step and 32-step operating points; arrows state 4.2x and 3.4x latency comparisons. FID and latency are point estimates with no error expression, and the chart is a representative positioning view rather than the complete Table 1 matrix.
figures.evidence_relation: Abstract and §1 latency claim → Figure 1 quality–latency positioning → Table 1 supplies the full FID/steps/latency/throughput rows → §3.2 matched raster counterparts and step reductions.
design_strengths: A direct quality–cost frontier makes the headline speed claim scannable.
Bubble-size key and direct method labels avoid a large method legend.
The log-like latency axis keeps sub-second and multi-second regimes in one view.
design_weaknesses: Arrow comparisons require the reader to match model scale and step setting manually.
No uncertainty, sample denominator, or seed information is shown in the headline view.
Baseline points combine heterogeneous generative families, so the frontier is not a controlled same-architecture comparison.
figures.reusable_pattern: Use a quality–cost scatter with a scale key, direct method labels, and explicit arrows for the operating-point comparison; pair it with a complete table that exposes the protocol.

figures.label: Figure 2

caption.text: Figure 2: Visualization of attention maps in the LLAMAGEN-1.4B model. There is strong spatial locality, as the attention of a decoding token is concentrated on nearby spatial tokens. LLAMAGEN encodes images into 24 × 24 tokens, where a token that is 24 positions earlier in the attention map corresponds to the token directly above it in the 2D grid.

color.semantic_mapping: Green intensity represents attention magnitude in per-head maps; red arrows call out local concentration. Each map has its own 0–1 colorbar.

plot_grammar.legend_placement: individual colorbars to the right of maps

encodings.x: Token index in the attention map
encodings.y: Token index in the attention map
encodings.facet: Head 1, Head 2, Head 17, Head 8, Head 18, Head 23, and Head 24
encodings.text: Head labels, 0–1 colorbars, and Locality annotations

figures.data_and_statistics: Seven rendered attention heatmaps from LLAMAGEN-1.4B: three large maps (Heads 1, 2, 17) and four smaller maps (Heads 8, 18, 23, 24). The caption states a 24×24 image-token representation and that a 24-position offset corresponds to the token above in the 2D grid. No aggregation, uncertainty, or sample/step denominator is provided.
figures.evidence_relation: §2.3 locality diagnostic → Figure 2 visualizes local attention in selected heads → Figure 7 aggregates distance/head behavior → Algorithm 1 and Figure 8 operationalize the two locality principles.
design_strengths: Colorbars and head titles make the spatial-locality pattern inspectable without relying on prose alone.
A full-width strip juxtaposes representative heads with small supporting heads.
The caption links sequence offset to a 2D spatial interpretation.
design_weaknesses: The caption does not identify the layer, decoding step, or aggregation used for the displayed maps.
Tiny right-hand maps and repeated colorbars impose high visual decoding cost.
Color is the primary magnitude channel; luminance helps grayscale reading but exact values remain difficult to recover.
figures.reusable_pattern: Pair a few enlarged mechanism heatmaps with smaller head-level examples, annotate the key local pattern directly, and define the sequence-to-spatial mapping in the caption.

figures.label: Figure 3

caption.text: Figure 3: Raster Order vs. Flexible Parallelized Autoregressive Modeling. (a) In raster order, each token simultaneously provides context and predicts the next token, restricting flexibility and efficiency. (b) Our approach decouples these roles: previously generated tokens supply context, while position query tokens drive parallel generation at arbitrary target positions. This separation enables both flexible order and efficient parallelization.

color.semantic_mapping: Condition, image-token, no-prediction, and position-query roles use muted tile/fill colors; arrows and transformer boxes remain neutral.

encodings.y: Context/query path through the autoregressive transformer
encodings.shape: Token tiles, transformer block, and role swatches
encodings.line: Arrows from inputs to the transformer and predicted positions
encodings.text: <C>, image tokens, P-position queries, step labels, and role legend

figures.data_and_statistics: Two conceptual panels. Panel (a) couples each raster token to context and next-token prediction. Panel (b) shows context tokens 4, 3, 5 and position queries P4/P3/P5/P1/P2/P6 enabling arbitrary target groups and parallel steps. This is an architectural interface diagram, not measured data.
figures.evidence_relation: Eq. (1) serial factorization and §2.1 bottleneck → Figure 3 decouples context from target queries → Figures 4–5 specify masks → Figure 6 compares cache semantics.
design_strengths: Side-by-side panels make the role separation concrete before the mask equations.
The role legend, direct labels, and arrows provide redundant decoding cues.
The flexible panel visibly connects arbitrary order to group-level parallel prediction.
design_weaknesses: Very small token thumbnails and labels are difficult at normal page zoom.
The diagram shows the interface but not computational cost, cache size, or a concrete measured step schedule.
The muted categorical palette has weak grayscale separation for some token tiles.
figures.reusable_pattern: Introduce a new sequence model with a matched baseline panel, explicit role legend, and an end-to-end token flow before showing the formal mask.

figures.label: Figure 4

caption.text: Figure 4: Illustration of the training attention mask. Context Attention allows subsequent tokens to attend to the context tokens causally. Query Attention ensures mutual visibility among the position query tokens within the same step, and prevents any subsequent tokens from attending to the query tokens. For example, image token 4 can be attended to by all subsequent tokens, including image tokens and position query tokens, to provide context information. The two position query tokens P3 and P5 in the same generation step attend to the condition, to the image token 4, and to each other, while ignoring the earlier query P4.

color.semantic_mapping: Teal cells encode Context Attention and yellow cells encode Query Attention; white cells are masked. The Key swatches and cell geometry provide redundant role cues.

encodings.x: Key/token positions in the interleaved training sequence
encodings.y: Query rows and token rows in the training sequence
encodings.color: Context Attention versus Query Attention versus blocked cells
encodings.text: <C>, P4, 4, P3, P5, 3, 5, P1, P2, P6, 1, 2, 6; Context/Query Attention key

figures.data_and_statistics: A 13×13 training attention mask. Green/teal cells allow causal context visibility; orange/yellow cells provide mutual visibility among same-step position queries; blank cells block attention. The example explicitly highlights P3/P5 mutual visibility and token 4 as context.
figures.evidence_relation: §2.2 training formulation → Figure 4 instantiates the specialized Context/Query Attention mask → Figure 5 fuses encoding and decoding at inference → Figure 6 contrasts prior cache arrangements.
design_strengths: The square matrix exposes visibility as a local, auditable rule rather than an abstract verbal claim.
A compact two-color key and explicit row/column token labels make the mask reconstructible.
The caption walks through a concrete P3/P5/token-4 example.
design_weaknesses: The 13×13 matrix is dense and requires tracking repeated position labels across both axes.
The caption does not state a formal matrix convention such as row=query and column=key.
Teal/yellow identity depends on color despite the grid and key supplying only partial redundancy.
figures.reusable_pattern: Show a concrete small attention-mask matrix with row/column token labels, a role key, and one worked visibility example before generalizing the rule.

figures.label: Figure 5

caption.text: Figure 5: Illustration of the inference attention mask. Encoding with image tokens and Decoding with position query tokens can be fused into a single step. Taking step 2 in Figure 3 (b) as the example, it simultaneously encodes the previously generated image tokens 3, 5 to update the KV-cache and decodes the desired image tokens 1, 2 and 6 in parallel.

color.semantic_mapping: Teal cells encode cached/context attention and yellow cells encode parallel query attention; white cells are blocked.

encodings.x: Cache keys (<C>,4,3,5) followed by query keys P1,P2,P6
encodings.y: Rows for encoded image tokens 3,5 and decoded queries P1,P2,P6
encodings.text: Cache, Key, Query, token IDs, and KV-cache labels

figures.data_and_statistics: A compact 5×7 inference mask for the step-2 example from Figure 3(b). Previously generated image tokens 3 and 5 update the KV cache while P1/P2/P6 decode in parallel; query KV entries are not stored. It is a mechanism diagram, not a sampled statistic.
figures.evidence_relation: §2.2 inference formulation and Figure 3(b) → Figure 5 shows one fused encode/decode step → Figure 6(c) claims generated-token-only caching → Table 1/2 measure the resulting system cost.
design_strengths: The cache/key split and simultaneous query rows expose why encoding and decoding can be fused.
The small matrix is easier to inspect than Figure 4 while preserving the concrete token example.
Caption states the exact generated/context token IDs and KV-cache action.
design_weaknesses: No legend explains the two fills; the reader must infer their meaning from Figure 4 or the caption prose.
The matrix does not show the preceding or following step, so cache evolution is only implicit.
Color remains the primary role cue, with no hatching or line-style alternative.
figures.reusable_pattern: Use a reduced inference mask tied to one named decoding step, explicitly separating cached keys from query keys and stating which entries persist.

figures.label: Figure 6

caption.text: Figure 6: Comparison with other methods. (a) Encoder–decoder approaches such as SAR and ARPG generate tokens independently, since query tokens contribute no key–value pairs. (b) Decoder-only methods like RANDAR rely on positional instruction tokens, but the causal mask reduces parallel generation to batched next-token prediction and forces instruction tokens to be cached, doubling memory. (c) In contrast, our method employs a specialized training mask that ensures mutual visibility among concurrently predicted tokens while caching only the generated tokens.

color.semantic_mapping: Teal/green cells indicate cached context and yellow cells indicate query attention; panel-specific dashed boxes and headings identify SAR/ARPG, RandAR, and LPD.

encodings.x: Cache and target-key positions in each method
encodings.shape: Matrix cells and dashed cache boxes
encodings.text: Encoder KV Cache, positional instruction token, KV Cache, method labels, and token IDs

figures.data_and_statistics: Three aligned attention/cache diagrams. (a) Encoder–decoder SAR/ARPG uses query rows without query key–value pairs. (b) RandAR caches positional instruction tokens and uses causal prediction. (c) LPD caches generated image tokens and allows mutual visibility across P1/P2/P6 queries. No quantitative values are plotted.
figures.evidence_relation: §2.2 comparison with SAR/ARPG/RandAR → Figure 6 isolates query-KV and instruction-cache differences → Figure 9(a) tests flexible modeling under random order → Tables 1–3 report system-level outcomes.
design_strengths: Three panels align the competing cache semantics on the same visual grammar.
Dashed cache outlines and role labels make the memory claim visible without equations.
The caption states both the failure mode of prior methods and the LPD contrast.
design_weaknesses: Panel labels and token indices are small, especially in the RandAR center panel.
The diagram asserts mechanism differences but does not quantify memory or compute reduction.
Color semantics are local to this figure and not fully standardized with Figure 4/5 fills.
figures.reusable_pattern: Compare alternative architectures by holding a small cache/attention matrix constant and marking the exact state that is stored or mutually visible.

figures.label: Figure 7

caption.text: Figure 7: Attention Analysis of LLAMAGEN. (a) Attention diminishes with distance (b) Spatial locality is consistently observed in all heads.

color.semantic_mapping: Red triangles, green squares, and blue circles distinguish LlamaGen-L/XL/XXL across both panels.

encodings.shape: Triangle, square, and circle markers for model scale
encodings.line: One solid line per model size

figures.data_and_statistics: Two descriptive line plots. Panel (a) shows per-token attention over relative distance 0–30, with a sharp fall near zero and a low tail. Panel (b) shows attention sum over Head ID 0–24, roughly 35–60% across heads. The three model sizes are point curves without error bars, intervals, or seed aggregation.
figures.evidence_relation: Eq. (3) proximity/attention diagnostic in §2.3 → Figure 7 tests distance decay and head consistency → principles motivate Algorithm 1 thresholds → Figure 8 visualizes the resulting order.
design_strengths: The two panels separate distance decay from across-head consistency.
Marker shape and color redundantly identify the three model sizes.
Axes and units are explicit, so the locality diagnostic can be read without the surrounding paragraph.
design_weaknesses: The caption omits the layer, sample set, aggregation, and denominator used for attention percentages.
The right panel is visually noisy and supports consistency only descriptively, not as a statistical test.
The plot is placed beside dense prose, leaving limited width for tick and legend text.
figures.reusable_pattern: Use paired diagnostic panels for a mechanism: one panel tests the proposed distance relationship and another checks whether it persists across model components.

figures.label: Figure 8

caption.text: Figure 8: Illustration of different generation order schedules. All schedules leverage 20 decoding steps for 162 tokens. Dark green marks newly selected grids and light green marks those already selected. Compared to others, our schedule selects grids close to previous ones and far from concurrent ones, maximizing the contextual support and minimizing the mutual dependency.

color.semantic_mapping: Dark green marks newly selected grid cells and light green marks cells selected earlier; white cells remain unselected.

encodings.x: Eight displayed decoding checkpoints: Step1, Step2, Step4, Step6, Step9, Step12, Step15, Step18
encodings.color: Dark green=newly selected; light green=already selected
encodings.facet: Raster, Random, Halton, and LPD rows

figures.data_and_statistics: A 4×8 schedule grid over 162 image-token positions. Rows show raster, random, Halton, and LPD orders; columns show eight checkpoints from a 20-step schedule. The figure encodes selection history, not FID or latency, and contains no uncertainty or measured aggregate.
figures.evidence_relation: Algorithm 1 proximity selection plus farthest-point completion → Figure 8 provides spatial intuition for the order → Tables 1–3/Figure 9 test quality and efficiency → Appendix Table 6 varies τ and ρ.
design_strengths: The same checkpoints make all four order schedules directly comparable.
Dark/light state encoding preserves temporal history in each cell.
The dense grid gives a concrete visual explanation for the proximity/repulsion objective.
design_weaknesses: Thirty-two small grids are information-dense and difficult to inspect quantitatively.
The caption does not define how 162 positions map to image coordinates or how checkpoint columns relate to the 20 omitted steps.
The green palette has no numeric scale, so the figure supports intuition rather than exact schedule recovery.
figures.reusable_pattern: For an ordering algorithm, show identical spatial checkpoints for baseline and proposed schedules, using a two-tone history encoding and explicit row/column labels.

figures.label: Figure 9

caption.text: Figure 9: Ablation Studies. All ablation experiments are conducted with XL size models on 256×256 resolution. (a) Effectiveness of flexible parallelized autoregressive modeling. (b) Effectiveness of locality-aware generation order schedule. (c) Effectiveness of the locality principles.

color.semantic_mapping: Gray curves/bars identify controls and red identifies LPD; panels use marker/legend labels for RandAR, ARPG, Random, Halton, Principle 1, Principle 2, and LPD.

encodings.x: Generation Steps in panels (a,b); method/principle category in panel (c)
encodings.color: Control methods in gray/blue-gray versus LPD in red
encodings.shape: Circle, diamond, and triangle curve markers; bars in panel (c)
encodings.facet: (a) flexible modeling; (b) order schedule; (c) locality principles
encodings.text: Legend labels, panel letters, and numeric bar values 2.11/2.00/2.06/1.92

figures.data_and_statistics: Three XL 256×256 ablations. (a) LPD, RandAR, and ARPG under a common random order across 16–256 steps; (b) Random, Halton, and LPD across 16–64 steps; (c) LPD-XL at 32 steps with Random FID 2.11, Principle 1 only 2.00, Principle 2 only 2.06, and combined LPD 1.92. Curves and bars are point estimates with no uncertainty.
figures.evidence_relation: §4 ablation questions → Figure 9 controls generation order in (a), substitutes schedules in (b), and removes locality principles in (c) → Table 6 checks τ/ρ sensitivity → main Tables 1–3 report end-to-end outcomes.
design_strengths: The three panels map cleanly to architecture, schedule, and principle-level mechanisms.
Random-order control in panel (a) isolates mutual visibility from the proposed schedule.
Panel (c) prints exact bar values, making the joint principle comparison auditable.
design_weaknesses: Panel captions do not state the sample count, seed policy, or aggregation behind each FID curve.
The shared visual grammar still requires three separate legends and different x ranges.
The tiny plot text and bar annotations are fragile at page scale.
figures.reusable_pattern: Organize ablations from component removal to mechanism substitute to joint principle test, keeping model, resolution, and x/y metrics explicit in the caption.

figures.label: Figure 10

caption.text: Figure 10: More visualization of attention maps in the LLAMAGEN-1.4B model.

color.semantic_mapping: Per-head attention magnitude uses a pale-to-dark green scale with a colorbar beside each heatmap.

plot_grammar.legend_placement: individual colorbars beside each head map

encodings.facet: 24 heatmaps, Heads 1–24, in the first additional layer shown in Appendix C

figures.data_and_statistics: A 4×6 array of 24 attention heatmaps for Heads 1–24. Appendix C states that two layers are selected during decoding; Figure 10 is the first additional layer, but the caption does not name the layer or aggregation. No uncertainty or denominator is shown.
figures.evidence_relation: Figure 2 selected-head locality illustration → Appendix C expands the two selected layers as Figures 10 and 11 → Figure 7 remains the only aggregate diagnostic connected to the schedule.
design_strengths: The complete head sweep exposes heterogeneity that the main strip only samples.
The repeated 24-head layout gives a stable visual comparison across heads.
Colorbars are present for reading local magnitude rather than only structural patterns.
design_weaknesses: The caption is title-only and omits layer identity, tokenization context, and decoding condition.
Repeated tiny colorbars and axis labels make exact cross-head comparison expensive.
A qualitative map array cannot establish the stability of locality without repeated samples or an aggregate statistic.
figures.reusable_pattern: Move complete component-level heatmap sweeps to an appendix while keeping the main figure as a small representative selection; name layer and aggregation in the caption.

figures.label: Figure 11

caption.text: Figure 11: More visualization of attention maps in the LLAMAGEN-1.4B model.

color.semantic_mapping: Per-head attention magnitude uses a pale-to-dark green scale with a colorbar beside each heatmap.

plot_grammar.legend_placement: individual colorbars beside each head map

encodings.facet: 24 heatmaps, Heads 1–24, in the second additional layer shown in Appendix C

figures.data_and_statistics: A second 4×6 array of 24 attention heatmaps for Heads 1–24. Together with Figure 10 it covers two selected layers, but no layer number, sample, step, or aggregation is stated in the caption. Values are descriptive point visualizations without uncertainty.
figures.evidence_relation: Figure 2 partial attention maps → Appendix C text calls Figures 10 and 11 the two-layer expansion → Figure 7 summarizes distance/head behavior but does not quantify this layer split.
design_strengths: The paired figure preserves identical head ordering, enabling visual layer-to-layer comparison.
Large full-page placement gives the dense heatmaps enough raster resolution for structural inspection.
The sequential scale consistently emphasizes high-attention diagonals and local bands.
design_weaknesses: Figure 11 repeats the title-only caption and depends on surrounding Appendix C prose for its experimental identity.
Per-head colorbars and tiny axes obscure small differences between layers.
No numeric summary or uncertainty links the qualitative variation to the algorithmic thresholds.
figures.reusable_pattern: Use a matched second heatmap array for a layer or condition only when the caption names the contrast; otherwise the visual duplication is hard to audit.

figures.label: Figure 12

caption.text: Figure 12: Generation Examples of Our Model. We show 512×512 generation samples (top), 256×256 generation samples (middle) and zero-shot image editing results including class-conditional editing, inpainitng and outpainting (bottom).

color.semantic_mapping: Natural image content carries no quantitative color semantic; red rectangles mark edited/masked regions in the bottom panels.

encodings.color: Natural image content; red edit-region boxes
encodings.shape: Image tiles and red rectangular masks
encodings.text: No image labels; group meaning is stated in the caption and nearby prose

figures.data_and_statistics: A qualitative montage sourced from a 1550×1050 PNG asset: three large 512×512 samples at top, two rows of 256×256 samples in the middle, and two rows of class-conditional/inpainting/outpainting edits with red regions at bottom (27 tiles total). No quality metric, success denominator, seed, or failure case is given.
figures.evidence_relation: §3.2 and Appendix D claim arbitrary-order editing → Figure 12 shows generation, class-conditional editing, inpainting, and outpainting examples → Table 3/7 quantify only text-to-image GenEval, not editing.
design_strengths: The top/middle/bottom grouping communicates resolution and task progression without a complex legend.
Red edit boxes make the altered region visible on top of natural image content.
The examples connect the arbitrary-order mechanism to a concrete capability surface.
design_weaknesses: Qualitative success is not paired with an editing metric, human judgment, or failure denominator.
The caption contains the paper typo “inpainitng” and does not identify prompts or sampling conditions.
Natural-image palette is visually rich but cannot serve as a controlled encoding or grayscale-safe semantic key.
figures.reusable_pattern: Group qualitative examples by resolution and task, mark manipulated regions directly, and pair capability montages with a quantitative success/failure table when making a capability claim.

figures.label: Figure 13

caption.text: Figure 13: Generation Examples of Our Model. We show 1024×1024 text-to-image generation samples.

color.semantic_mapping: Natural image colors are incidental; black/gray prompt text is paired above each generated image.

encodings.shape: Image tiles paired with prompt text

figures.data_and_statistics: Twelve 1024×1024 text-to-image samples arranged in a 3-column grid, each paired with a natural-language prompt. The montage demonstrates prompt diversity but has no per-prompt score, repeat count, seed, or failure example.
figures.evidence_relation: Appendix A.3 text-to-image recipe and Table 3 GenEval headline → Figure 13 supplies qualitative 1024×1024 examples → Table 7 decomposes GenEval categories but does not identify these individual samples.
design_strengths: Prompt text is placed directly beside each image, preserving image–conditioning linkage.
The 3-column grid supports quick inspection of diverse semantic and stylistic prompts.
The caption clearly limits the figure to 1024×1024 text-to-image samples.
design_weaknesses: No sample identifiers or prompt-to-evaluation linkage allow the montage to be audited quantitatively.
Prompt text is small and some lines wrap into dense multi-line blocks.
The figure is evidence of capability presentation, not a test of distributional quality or failure rate.
figures.reusable_pattern: Pair each qualitative generation with its prompt in a fixed grid, but attach sample IDs and quantitative or failure summaries if the montage supports a performance claim.

figures.label: Figure 14

caption.text: Figure 14: Throughput vs. Batch Size on ImageNet 256×256 Class-Conditional Generation. For LPD, we use 20 generation steps. Raster refers to the traditional fixed-raster-order generation model. We progressively increase the batch size until the process runs out of memory. The throughput values on the y-axis are plotted on a logarithmic scale.

color.semantic_mapping: Gray circles/lines are raster counterparts and red triangles/lines are LPD; each of the three model-scale panels has its own legend.

encodings.shape: Circle for Raster, triangle for LPD
encodings.text: Point throughput labels, Raster/LPD legends, and panel letters

figures.data_and_statistics: Three throughput-versus-batch-size panels for Raster-L/LPD-L, Raster-XL/LPD-XL, and Raster-XXL/LPD-XXL. Batch sizes increase until out-of-memory; the y-axis is logarithmic. Point labels report throughput, with no uncertainty or repeated-run information. The surrounding text identifies memory-bound behavior through batch 16 for LPD, around 128 for Raster, nearly 12x small-batch throughput, and about 3x at maximum feasible batch.
figures.evidence_relation: §3.3 position-query FLOP caveat → Figure 14 tests batch-regime efficiency → Table 1/2 provide batch-1 latency and batch-64 throughput snapshots → conclusion must retain the compute-bound boundary.
design_strengths: Log y-scale keeps sub-unit and high throughput values readable in one panel.
Matched Raster/LPD pairs across three model scales expose the batch-regime boundary.
Marker shape, color, direct values, and legends redundantly identify method and measurement.
design_weaknesses: Tiny point labels create severe clutter at high batch sizes.
The caption says values are collected until memory exhaustion but does not identify the GPU memory limit or replicate policy.
Categorical/equal-spaced batch checkpoints visually understate the numerical doubling unless the tick labels are read carefully.
figures.reusable_pattern: Show paired cost curves across the operational axis that changes the bottleneck, use a log scale when ranges span orders of magnitude, and state the stopping/OOM rule in the caption.

tables.label: Table 1

caption.text: Table 1: System-level comparison on ImageNet 256×256 class-conditional generation. We evaluate the generation quality by metrics including Fréchet inception distance (FID), inception score (IS), precision and recall. #Steps is the number of model runs needed to generate an image. We measure latency with a batch size of 1 and throughput with a batch size of 64 on a single NVIDIA A100 GPU under BFloat16 precision, with classifier-free guidance (CFG) for both.

tables.uncertainty: All FID/IS/precision/recall values are point estimates; the paper states FID uses 50,000 generated samples and latency averages 500 inference steps after 100 warm-up steps. No seed, dispersion, interval, or replicate count is shown. Dashes and OOM denote unavailable measurements rather than zeros.
tables.data_and_statistics: Ten columns: Type, Model, #Para., FID↓, IS↑, Precision↑, Recall↑, #Steps, Latency(s)↓, Throughput(img/s)↑. The 47 data rows group Diffusion (5), Mask (6), VAR (4), AR (10), earlier Parallelized AR (14), matched Raster Counterparts (3), and LPD (5). Mixed decimal precision is used across metrics; cyan fills mark the LPD rows.
tables.evidence_relation: Abstract/§3.2 step-and-quality headline → Table 1 places heterogeneous baselines, matched raster counterparts, and LPD 20/32-step rows on one decision surface → Figure 1 previews the quality–latency frontier → Appendix Tables 4–5 document configuration.
design_strengths: Quality, steps, latency, and throughput appear beside each other, supporting an explicit cost/quality decision.
Type groupings and horizontal rules preserve baseline-family structure in a wide comparison.
Cyan LPD rows make the proposed operating points easy to locate.
design_weaknesses: The ten-column, 47-row table is difficult to scan and requires manual matching by model scale.
Missing latency/throughput cells and OOM entries make cross-family efficiency comparison incomplete.
No uncertainty or seed columns accompany the headline values, and model parameter names later conflict with Appendix Table 4/A.3.
tables.reusable_pattern: Use a grouped wide table when one claim requires quality, step count, and system cost together; include explicit units, directions, missing-value semantics, and matched controls.

tables.label: Table 2

caption.text: Table 2: System-level comparison on ImageNet 512×512 class-conditional generation. Metrics and evaluation setup are the same as in Table 1.

tables.uncertainty: Point estimates only; the caption delegates metrics and evaluation setup to Table 1. No seeds, uncertainty, or repetition counts are reported. Dashes indicate unavailable measurements.
tables.data_and_statistics: Ten columns repeat Table 1: Type, Model, #Para., FID↓, IS↑, Precision↑, Recall↑, #Steps, Latency(s)↓, Throughput(img/s)↑. Thirteen rows cover diffusion, mask, VAR, AR, prior parallelized AR, raster counterparts, and LPD-L/XL at 48 steps. LPD rows are cyan-filled; decimal precision varies by metric column.
tables.evidence_relation: §3.2 512×512 extension and 1024→48-step claim → Table 2 tests matched raster versus LPD at 512×512 → Table 1 supplies the referenced protocol → Figure 14 expands the batch-dependent efficiency boundary.
design_strengths: The repeated header system makes the 512×512 comparison structurally comparable to Table 1.
LPD and raster rows are adjacent, so steps and FID can be matched quickly.
Metric-direction arrows and units remain visible in the header.
design_weaknesses: “Same as Table 1” shifts important setup details to another page.
The table still mixes baseline families with different missingness and no uncertainty.
The caption does not state the observed FID/throughput result, leaving the reader to derive the headline manually.
tables.reusable_pattern: Repeat a main comparison table only when the shared header/protocol is truly stable; otherwise repeat the key evaluation conditions in the caption.

tables.label: Table 3

caption.text: Table 3: System-level comparison on GenEval 1024×1024 text-to-image generation. Detailed per-category GenEval scores are provided in Table 7.

tables.uncertainty: GenEval, latency, and throughput are point estimates with no category-level uncertainty, seed, or repeat information.
tables.data_and_statistics: Seven columns: Type, Model, #Para., GenEval Score↑, #Steps, Latency(s)↓, Throughput(img/s)↑. Four rows compare Raster Counterpart-L/XL at 4096 steps with LPD-L/XL at 64 steps. Cyan LPD rows show scores .58/.62, latencies 1.01/1.53 s, and throughput 5.28/2.85 img/s; raster rows show .55/.60 and 64.7/93.8 s.
tables.evidence_relation: §3.2 high-resolution text-to-image extension → Table 3 joins GenEval score with 4096-versus-64 steps and system cost → Table 7 decomposes categories → Figure 13 supplies qualitative samples.
design_strengths: A compact table puts the high-resolution score and dramatic step/cost contrast in one unit.
The adjacent Table 7 pointer makes the aggregate-to-category route explicit.
Cyan rows preserve the same proposed-method cue as Tables 1–2.
design_weaknesses: The caption references Table 7 but does not define GenEval or explain the internal synthetic-data setting.
Four rows cannot establish uncertainty or category robustness.
The table’s narrow placement makes model identity and metric columns easy to misread at page scale.
tables.reusable_pattern: Keep a high-resolution extension table compact but report score, steps, and cost together, then link to category-level and qualitative follow-ups.

tables.label: Table 4

caption.text: Table 4: Model architecture configurations.

tables.uncertainty: Not applicable: deterministic architecture configuration values are listed without uncertainty.
tables.data_and_statistics: Five columns: Model, Parameters, Layers, Hidden Size, Heads. Rows list LPD-L (111M, 12, 1024, 12), LPD-XL (775M, 36, 1280, 20), and LPD-XXL (1.4B, 48, 1536, 48). Parameter counts conflict with main Tables 1–2 (337M/752M/1.4B) and A.3 text-to-image counts (344M/760M).
tables.evidence_relation: §3.1 names model scales and points to Appendix A.1 → Table 4 provides layer/hidden/head reproduction details → Tables 1–3 use different parameter counts, creating a cross-object identity boundary.
design_strengths: The compact five-column header directly exposes the architectural knobs that vary by scale.
Booktabs rules and aligned numeric columns keep configuration lookup fast.
The table is sufficient to reconstruct the listed decoder dimensions.
design_weaknesses: The caption is title-only and does not flag the parameter-count mismatch with the main text.
No notation or units distinguish parameter count conventions.
A reader must cross-check three sections to determine which model identity is being used.
tables.reusable_pattern: Use a compact architecture table with explicit units and an identity note whenever the same model names appear in multiple resolution or conditioning recipes.

tables.label: Table 5

caption.text: Table 5: Training hyper-parameters for LPD-L on 256 × 256 resolution.

tables.uncertainty: Not applicable: this is a configuration key/value table, not an estimate table.
tables.data_and_statistics: Two columns (Hyper-parameters for 256×256 training, Configuration) and 11 key/value rows: AdamW; β1=.9; β2=.95; learning rate=8×10−4; batch size=2048 (64×32 GPUs); BFloat16; total epochs=450; warm-up=50; constant LR=350; cosine decay=50; offsets=random per-sample. Values mix scalar, textual, and unit-bearing formats.
tables.evidence_relation: Appendix A.2 training recipe → Table 5 makes the LPD-L 256×256 configuration inspectable → §3.1 and Tables 1–2 define the evaluation context → source code provides implementation but not the full training artifact.
design_strengths: Key/value layout is appropriate for heterogeneous optimizer, precision, epoch, and offset fields.
The header identifies the resolution and the configuration column clearly.
The table complements the main result protocol without adding visual clutter.
design_weaknesses: The caption does not repeat the optimizer, effective-LR footnote, or multi-GPU batch interpretation.
Mixed textual and numeric values prevent a uniform precision audit.
Only LPD-L is listed while LPD-XL/XXL reuse some settings by prose, making inheritance implicit.
tables.reusable_pattern: Use a two-column configuration table for mixed hyperparameters, and state which rows are inherited or scaled for other model variants.

tables.label: Table 6

caption.text: Table 6: Sensitivity analysis of τ and ρ. All experiments use LPD-XL with 32 decoding steps on ImageNet 256×256. Default values (τ = 2, ρ = 1) are underlined.

tables.uncertainty: FID point estimates only; no seed, replicate, or uncertainty expression is supplied. Underlining identifies default τ=2 and ρ=1; the bold 1.92 values are the lowest displayed values in each sweep.
tables.data_and_statistics: Two side-by-side sensitivity panels. (a) Vary τ at fixed ρ=1: τ=0,1,2,3,4 gives FID 2.00,1.94,1.92,1.97,2.00. (b) Vary ρ at fixed τ=2: ρ=0,.2,.5,1,1.5,2 gives FID 1.94,1.94,1.93,1.92,2.00,2.04. The FID column is two decimals; threshold headers mix integers and one-decimal values.
tables.evidence_relation: Algorithm 1 thresholds τ/ρ → Appendix B.3 explains proximity/repulsion tradeoffs → Table 6 tests each threshold one-at-a-time → Figure 9(c) shows the combined principle effect.
design_strengths: Side-by-side sweeps isolate the two threshold knobs while holding the other fixed.
Defaults and best values are marked directly rather than hidden in prose.
The caption names model, step count, resolution, and default values.
design_weaknesses: One FID row per panel cannot show run-to-run variation or a response surface.
The two mini-table header conventions are compact but require careful alignment.
The caption does not state whether the selected FID is from one run or an aggregate.
tables.reusable_pattern: Use matched one-parameter sweeps with fixed-condition subtitles, explicit default markers, and a statistic/replicate note in the caption.

tables.label: Table 7

caption.text: Table 7: Detailed per-category GenEval scores for text-to-image generation at 1024×1024 resolution.

tables.uncertainty: GenEval category scores are point estimates with no category-level intervals, seeds, or replicate counts. Cyan rows identify LPD variants.
tables.data_and_statistics: Eight columns: Model, Overall, Single Obj., Two Obj., Counting, Colors, Position, Color Attr. Four rows compare Raster Counterpart-L/XL and LPD-L/XL. Scores use two decimals; LPD-XL has overall .62, single-object .99, two-object .76, counting .45, colors .82, position .34, and color attribute .37.
tables.evidence_relation: Table 3 aggregate GenEval claim → Table 7 decomposes it into seven categories → Figure 13 provides unscored 1024×1024 examples → no per-sample linkage or uncertainty is supplied.
design_strengths: Category headers make the aggregate GenEval score decomposable.
Raster and LPD rows are grouped and cyan LPD fills match main-table semantics.
Two-decimal precision is consistent across the score columns.
design_weaknesses: Abbreviated headers such as “Single Obj.” and “Color Attr.” are not expanded in the caption.
Point scores do not establish stability of the category differences.
The table is not linked to particular images or prompts in Figure 13.
tables.reusable_pattern: Place aggregate and category-level metrics in adjacent linked objects, with full metric names, consistent precision, and sample/replicate definitions.

cross_object_system.visual_narrative: Figure 1 opens with the quality–latency headline, Figure 2 motivates spatial locality, Figure 3 separates context from position queries, Figures 4–6 specify masks/cache and compare prior methods, Figure 7 quantifies locality, and Figure 8 makes the order schedule spatially concrete. Tables 1–3 then test quality/steps/cost at 256, 512, and 1024 resolutions; Figure 9 attributes gains to architecture/order/principles. Appendix Tables 4–7 and Figures 10–14 expose configurations, threshold sensitivity, additional heads, qualitative capabilities, per-category GenEval, and batch-regime cost.
cross_object_system.caption_system: Main captions use a bold descriptive title followed by setup, comparison, and sometimes a direct finding. Figures 1–9 generally name the task and visual encoding, while Tables 1–3 define metric directions/units and profiling context. Appendix Figures 10/11 are title-only and Figures 12/13/14 are more self-contained, but none defines seed/replicate or qualitative sampling boundaries.
cross_object_system.table_header_system: Tables 1–2 share a 10-column one-level system header with Type/Model, parameter count, quality metrics, steps, latency, and throughput; Table 3 uses a seven-column GenEval/cost header. Appendix Table 4 is a five-column architecture header, Table 5 is a key/value configuration table, Table 6 is two one-row threshold sweeps, and Table 7 is an eight-column category score table. Down/up arrows, units, booktabs rules, cyan method fills, and occasional underlines carry most semantics.
cross_object_system.method_result_ablation_link: Figures 3–6 make flexible parallelized AR and generated-token caching inspectable; Figure 7 supplies the locality diagnostic and Figure 8 shows the schedule. Tables 1–3 connect those mechanisms to FID/GenEval, step count, latency, and throughput. Figure 9 separates flexible modeling, schedule choice, and the two locality principles, while Table 6 tests τ/ρ sensitivity and Figure 14 exposes the compute-bound cost boundary.
cross_object_system.main_appendix_link: Main text calls Appendix A for dimensions/training/text-to-image details, Appendix B for schedule code/distinction/sensitivity, Appendix C for Figures 10/11, Appendix D for Figures 12/13 and Table 7, and Appendix E for Figure 14. The links complete implementation and cost context, but model parameter identities differ across main tables, Table 4, and A.3.
cross_object_system.typography_consistency: Captions and tables use a stable Nimbus Roman/Computer Modern family with roughly 6.97pt table interiors and 9.96pt caption/body text. Graphic labels switch to Helvetica Neue-like sans fonts and can fall to 3–5pt in Figures 3, 8–11, and 14. The ICLR two-column template is stable, but dense appendix heatmaps and point labels are the main legibility risk.
cross_object_system.color_consistency: Teal/yellow attention roles recur in Figures 4–6; green intensity recurs in Figures 2, 8, 10, and 11; red marks LPD or editing regions in Figures 1, 7, 9, 12, and 14; cyan fills mark LPD rows in Tables 1–3 and 7. Within-object shape/labels usually add redundancy, but natural-image figures have no semantic palette and the cross-object colors are not formally documented in source.

most_reusable_patterns: Start with a direct quality–latency scatter, then provide a wide table with matched model/step/cost rows so the headline can be audited.
Use matched baseline/proposed attention-mask and cache matrices with role colors, labels, and one worked visibility example.
Make a mechanism diagnostic and its operational schedule adjacent: Figure 7 measures locality while Figure 8 shows how it changes order selection.
Organize ablations from architecture control to schedule substitute to joint principles, and follow with one-parameter threshold sensitivity.
Plot paired cost curves across batch regimes and state the OOM stopping rule to delimit efficiency claims.
highest_value_objects: Figure 1 plus Table 1, because they connect the headline quality–latency frontier to complete system-level rows.
Figures 3–6, because the token/query, mask, cache, and prior-method contrasts form the clearest method interface.
Figure 7 plus Figure 8, because the locality diagnostic is translated into an inspectable generation schedule.
Figure 9 plus Table 6, because they separate component, schedule, and threshold mechanisms.
Figure 14, because it retains the compute-bound caveat that qualifies the small-batch speedup.
failure_patterns: No figure or table reports uncertainty, seeds, replicate counts, or statistical aggregation beyond the stated FID sample count and latency averaging protocol.
Figures 10/11 are dense 24-head arrays with title-only captions; layer, sample, step, and aggregation identities remain implicit.
Qualitative editing and text-to-image montages demonstrate capability without success/failure denominators or prompt/sample linkage.
Main, Appendix Table 4, and text-to-image A.3 use inconsistent parameter counts for similarly named LPD models.
The local inventory was stale and the public repository lacks generators for most plots/tables; only two rendered assets and schedule-support code are exact public visual sources.
final_judgment.one_sentence_visual_strategy: Build a mechanism-to-result chain from quality–latency positioning through query/mask/cache diagrams and locality-driven scheduling, then place matched system tables, causal ablations, qualitative examples, and batch-regime curves so both the speed claim and its hardware/statistical boundaries remain visible.
